chunks: Microarchitecture vs ISA. The question: What is the difference between microarchitecture and ISA?
The ISA is what software can see and rely on: the instructions, the registers, how memory behaves.
Microarchitecture is how one particular chip delivers that: how deep its pipeline is, how big its caches are, how many instructions it handles at once.
The ISA stays stable, so old programs keep working. The microarchitecture is where speed and power are won.
Picture a wall outlet. The plug shape and voltage are the standard, so any appliance works in any outlet.
Behind the wall, the power can come from a small local generator or a huge grid. Appliances can't tell which, except that the supply may be stronger.
The outlet standard is the ISA, and what lies behind it is the microarchitecture.
The ISA is the narrow waist. Everything above it is portable across implementations and everything below it is free to change.
Performance, power and area are mostly decided below the line, while compatibility is decided at it.
ISA: the contract between software and hardware ("What is an ISA?") Microarchitecture: one chip's internal design that implements the ISA ("What is microarchitecture?")
Binary compatibility: the same compiled program runs on every chip that implements the ISA.
Architectural state: the registers, program counter (the address of the next instruction) and memory that the ISA defines and software can see.
Out-of-order execution: running instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, while results still appear in program order.
Run 10 to the 9 instructions on two chips that share one ISA. Old core A runs at 2 gigahertz with CPI 1. 6 (cycles per instruction), so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1.
6 over (2 times 10 to the 9) equals 0. 8 seconds. New core B runs at 3 gigahertz with CPI 1. 1, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1. 1 over (3 times 10 to the 9) about 0.
367 seconds. That is about 2. 2 times faster, and the same compiled program was used with no changes.
That is the whole idea: a stable ISA lets hardware improve under the software.
"The ISA is the contract software sees: instructions, registers, memory model, exceptions.
The microarchitecture is how one chip implements that contract: pipeline, issue width, caches, branch predictor.
One ISA, like x86 or Arm, has many microarchitectures, from tiny in-order cores to wide out-of-order ones, and they all run the same binaries.
That split lets hardware improve every generation without breaking software."
